items.followUp: Compare the structure and function of the primary and secondary cell walls.

rubric.why: Identifies a key feature of the primary cell wall.
rubric.description: States that the primary cell wall is thin or flexible.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either feature correctly linked to the primary cell wall.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the secondary cell wall from the primary cell wall.
rubric.description: States that the secondary wall is thick, often lignified, or formed after cell growth.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct distinguishing feature.

modelAnswer: The primary cell wall is thin and flexible, and is formed while the cell is growing.
The secondary cell wall is thicker, is often strengthened with lignin, and forms inside the primary wall after growth stops.

items.followUp: What are two characteristics of a scientific hypothesis?

rubric.why: A hypothesis must be capable of being checked through investigation.
rubric.description: States that a good hypothesis is testable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for clearly identifying testability.

rubric.why: A hypothesis should make a clear prediction that can be investigated and should relate to observations or evidence.
rubric.description: Gives another valid characteristic, such as making a prediction or being based on observations or evidence.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one valid characteristic.

modelAnswer: A good hypothesis is clear and testable.
It makes a prediction and is based on observations or evidence.

items.followUp: Name the four main types of animal tissues and the two broad categories of plant tissues.

rubric.why: These are the two broad categories of plant tissues.
rubric.description: Names meristematic and permanent tissues in plants.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when both categories are given.

rubric.why: These are the four main types of animal tissues.
rubric.description: Names epithelial, connective, muscular, and nervous tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when all four types are given.

modelAnswer: Plant tissues are meristematic and permanent tissues.
Animal tissues are epithelial, connective, muscular, and nervous tissues.

items.followUp: Define colonial cellular organization and give one example.

rubric.why: Colonial organization involves cells living together as a colony.
rubric.description: Defines a colony as a group of cells living together.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing cells grouped together in a colony.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates understanding of colonial organization.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example, such as Volvox.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: In colonial cellular organization, similar cells live together in a colony, while each cell can carry out its life functions.

items.followUp: What are prions and viroids made of, and why are they not placed in the five-kingdom classification?

rubric.why: The five-kingdom classification classifies cellular organisms, whereas prions and viroids are acellular.
rubric.description: States that prions and viroids lack cellular organization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as acellular or lacking cells.

rubric.why: Their non-cellular nature and unusual composition explain why they are not assigned to a kingdom.
rubric.description: Identifies prions as infectious proteins and viroids as small RNA molecules, or states that the five-kingdom system classifies cellular organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation or the correct compositions of both.

modelAnswer: Prions and viroids are acellular and therefore are not included among the cellular organisms classified in the five-kingdom system.
Prions are infectious proteins, whereas viroids are small RNA molecules.

items.followUp: Where do the light reactions of photosynthesis occur, and what products are formed?

rubric.why: Light reactions require light energy and take place in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.
rubric.description: States that these reactions require light and/or occur in the grana or thylakoid membranes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the light requirement or correct location.

rubric.why: Light energy is converted into chemical energy, and oxygen is released when water is split.
rubric.description: Gives products or outcomes of the light reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming valid products or outcomes, such as oxygen, ATP, or NADPH.

modelAnswer: Light reactions are the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis; they occur in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.
Light energy is used to split water, releasing oxygen and producing ATP and NADPH.

items.followUp: Name the two main types of fermentation and give one product of each.

rubric.why: Alcoholic fermentation is one of the two main types.
Lactic acid fermentation is the other main type.

modelAnswer: The two main types of fermentation are alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.

items.followUp: Define an enzyme substrate and the products of an enzyme-controlled reaction.

rubric.why: A substrate is the substance on which an enzyme acts.
rubric.description: Defines a substrate in relation to the enzyme that acts on it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the substrate is acted upon by an enzyme.

rubric.why: Products are the substances formed by a reaction.
rubric.description: Defines products as substances formed in a reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition of products.

modelAnswer: A substrate is the substance on which an enzyme acts.
Products are the substances formed as a result of a reaction.
